task.prompt:
The stored procedure is named sp and takes five parameters in this exact order: para_Year_Join (NUMBER), para_Artist_ID (NUMBER), para_Ticket_Price (NUMBER), para_Year (NUMBER), and para_Exhibition_ID (NUMBER). It does the artist pass and then the exhibition pass, in that order, and never commits or rolls back.

Phase 1: open a row-locking cursor over every artist row, no filter and no ordering. Fetch each row for update. Before changing it, keep its Artist_ID, Year_Join, and Age. Set that row's Year_Join to para_Year_Join, then set the same row's Age to the saved Age plus para_Year_Join minus the saved Year_Join, using the saved Artist_ID for the second update. Do this for all artist rows; don't change other artist columns.

Phase 2 starts after that. Open a row-locking cursor on exhibition for rows where Artist_ID is between para_Artist_ID and para_Ticket_Price, inclusive, with no ordering, and fetch each selected row for update. Check Ticket_Price. If it's not null, set that exhibition row's Year to para_Year. If it's null, just insert into exhibition_record with only Exhibition_ID set to para_Exhibition_ID. If that insert raises DUP_VAL_ON_INDEX, update exhibition_record where Exhibition_ID equals para_Exhibition_ID and set Attendance to one more than its current Attendance.

The only exception handled is DUP_VAL_ON_INDEX from that insert. Any other exception that occurs is not caught and propagates out of the procedure. The exhibition_record column named NUMBER isn't read or written. Leave the transaction open; that's it.
